reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because the speaker promotes Forsage as a paid participation system requiring 400 TRX at registration, with earnings tied to personally referred partners and payments used to reopen slots. The presentation encourages viewers to keep upgrading and recruit others while projecting 130,560 TRX from a stated 12,800-TRX investment. These claims are presented as the speaker's promotional explanation of the platform.

opening.argument: The presentation does not state that every viewer will receive a return. Its most striking figures are introduced as a personal calculation and hypothetical exercise: the speaker says, "I want to compute, how much will I earn" and describes the exercise as something that will "excite" him. That framing matters: projected slot mathematics is not the same as reporting a completed outcome or guaranteeing one. The speaker also explains that the presentation was adapted with examples to make the mechanics easier to understand, supporting an illustrative rather than evidentiary reading. A careful viewer could therefore understand the figures as conditional examples of the advertised rules, subject to the system actually filling the positions, rather than as a promise of effortless profit.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The registration and referral quotes establish that the system has paid slots and referral-linked distributions, but they do not establish that the speaker represented a guaranteed result. The cited 130,560 figure is a calculation for a stated level, not evidence that the speaker achieved it or that every participant will. The reference argument also treats a hypothetical earnings illustration as a deceptive solicitation without addressing the speaker's explicit framing of it as something he planned to compute.

I just put in some examples, so that it is easier for us to understand the mechanics

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling the figures a personal calculation does not make the presentation a warning or neutral forecast. The speaker repeatedly presents the system as something viewers should join and earn from, including the stated registration payment and direct-referral income. The numerical examples are not isolated disclaimers; they are used to encourage progression through increasingly expensive slots. The presentation also says the speaker should level up because he will not regret the investment, which is promotional assurance rather than a meaningful risk warning.

opening.argument: The video's central activity is explaining how a blockchain-based matrix is structured. The speaker identifies the source presentation, says he added examples for clarity, defines decentralization, and walks through automated execution, slot positions, lines, percentages, and recycling. The supplied frames likewise show instructional diagrams and calculation tables, including a matrix layout and a slot-level computation. That is consistent with an operational demonstration of how the claimed platform works. Explaining a mechanism, even a controversial one, does not by itself prove that the explanation is a solicitation or that its claims are verified. The appropriate classification can therefore focus on the video's educational presentation of a technology and its stated rules.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The fact that the speaker explains mechanics does not make education the primary purpose. The explanation is specifically about buying slots, receiving payments through matrix positions, and recycling. The video ends by telling viewers to share the knowledge with people who can join and earn, which is an explicit participation objective. A tutorial format can still promote the system it teaches.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The instructional format is real, but it serves a recruitment-and-earnings pitch rather than neutral technology education. The speaker identifies the initial payment, explains that earnings depend on personally referred partners, and describes using a partner's payment to reopen the slot. The diagrams are not merely technical architecture; they show how participants and payments move through tiers. The closing invitation to join and earn confirms the practical purpose of the lesson.

opening.argument: The presentation can be read as describing access to a digital service with an automated payment and position system, not as documenting a fraudulent act. It emphasizes that execution occurs through a smart contract and that payments are automatically transferred when the stated criteria are met. The material supplied does not show the speaker requesting passwords, identity documents, or other credentials, nor does it document a completed loss or a fabricated transaction. The existence of prices, slot purchases, and referral rewards can occur in an ordinary commercial or promotional service. Without evidence of a credential request, impersonation, or proven nonperformance, the judge should not infer fraud merely from the platform's unusual business model.

citations.quote: There is no human administrator that makes this happen.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The issue is not whether the video requests passwords or proves a completed loss. Its own explanation identifies paid participation, positions filled by referred partners, and recycling payments into further slots. Those are the relevant commercial mechanics. Describing transfers as automated does not turn a recruitment-based payment structure into ordinary retail commerce, and the absence of a credential request does not answer whether the promoted earnings model is deceptive.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The absence of a password request is beside the point because the alleged mechanism is financial recruitment, not credential theft. The presentation directly links earnings to people the participant refers, requires an initial payment, and describes recycling and upgrading to continue receiving benefits. It also promotes extraordinary returns, including 10.2 times the investment for one level. Those facts distinguish this from ordinary commerce selling a product or service for its use value.
